title: 18-Year Terms for Supreme Court Justices
resolution: Resolved: The United States should limit Supreme Court justices to fixed 18-year terms.
summary: Justices serve "during good Behaviour," which in practice means for life. A common proposal would give each justice 18 years of active service, so each president would fill one seat every two years. Would it help the Court or hurt it?

background.p: Article III of the Constitution says federal judges "shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour." Justices may be removed only by impeachment, so they serve until they retire or die. The Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court reported in December 2021 that average service was about fifteen years until the late 1960s and has risen to roughly twenty-six years. The commission studied term limits in detail but took no position on whether to adopt them, and its members disagreed.

The most common proposal is a staggered 18-year term: with nine justices, one seat would open every two years, so each four-year presidential term would bring two appointments. Former justices would usually keep their salary and might serve on lower federal courts. A central question is whether this needs a constitutional amendment, which requires two-thirds of both houses of Congress and three-fourths of the states, or could be done by ordinary law. A Congressional Research Service report notes that many commentators believe an amendment is required, while some scholars argue a carefully written statute would be constitutional; no court has ruled on the question.

The idea has drawn support across the political spectrum at different times. In a July 2022 AP-NORC poll, 67 percent of U.S. adults favored a set term for justices. Nearly every state uses a term of years or a mandatory retirement age for its own high court.

disputed.q: Can Congress set 18-year terms by ordinary law?
positions: Many scholars, including some who favor term limits, say the Good Behaviour Clause guarantees life tenure, so a constitutional amendment is required.
Others argue that if justices keep their office and salary as judges and move to other federal courts after 18 years, a statute could satisfy the clause.

disputed.q: Would regular appointments make confirmation fights calmer or more frequent?
positions: Supporters say predictable openings would lower the stakes of each one, because no single seat could tip the Court for decades.
Critics say a seat on the ballot in every presidential and midterm cycle would make the Court a constant campaign issue.

terms.def: Article III's rule that federal judges hold office "during good Behaviour," generally read as life tenure unless impeached and removed.
Terms that start and end at different times, so members leave one by one instead of all at once.
A form of semi-retirement for federal judges, who keep their office and salary but take a lighter caseload.
The part of the Constitution describing how it can be amended.
The idea that judges should decide cases on the law without pressure from elected officials, voters or concern for their own careers.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Fixed 18-year terms would make appointments regular and fair, keep the Court connected to the country over time, and lower the stakes of each vacancy.

args.warrant: Under life tenure, vacancies come whenever a justice dies or retires. Some presidents appoint several justices in one term and others none, so the Court's makeup turns on luck and timing more than on elections.
args.evidence: Records of appointments by president; the CRS report's discussion of irregular vacancies; the presidential commission's report.
args.response: The negative answers that under the plan vacancies could still come early through death or resignation, and the Senate could still refuse to confirm, so regularity isn't guaranteed.

args.warrant: Average service has risen from about 15 years to roughly 26, and recent nominees have been in their late 40s and early 50s. One appointment can now shape the law for a generation, which raises the stakes of every vacancy.
args.evidence: The presidential commission's tenure figures; Brennan Center analysis of nominees' ages and service lengths.
args.response: The negative replies that long service brings experience and stability, and longer lives are a reason to value judges' wisdom, not to cut it short.

args.claim: It ends strategic retirements and service in poor health.
args.warrant: Justices sometimes time their retirement so a president of their choosing can replace them, or stay on while ill. A fixed term removes both incentives.
args.evidence: The CRS report's list of criticisms of life tenure, including declining health and strategic retirements; historical examples discussed by legal scholars.
args.response: The negative replies that a fixed term creates its own strategies, such as justices thinking about their next job as the term nears its end.

args.claim: Nearly every other high court has limits.
args.warrant: Almost every state supreme court and the top courts of other constitutional democracies use terms or retirement ages and still protect judicial independence. Their experience shows limits can work.
args.evidence: State constitutions on judicial terms; Brennan Center surveys of state and foreign high courts.
args.response: The negative answers that many states elect their judges, which is a different system, and that the U.S. Supreme Court's national role makes comparisons imperfect.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Life tenure protects judicial independence and stability, and term limits would bring new problems and a serious constitutional risk.

args.warrant: The framers gave judges tenure during good behavior so they could rule against popular opinion and powerful officials without fear for their jobs. A judge who must plan a next career may not be as free.
args.evidence: Federalist No. 78 on permanent tenure; the R Street Institute's 2018 analysis of conflicts of interest from post-Court careers.
args.response: The affirmative answers that 18 years with a guaranteed lifetime salary still protects independence, and most proposals let former justices keep serving as judges.

args.claim: It would make the Court a constant campaign issue.
args.warrant: If every presidential term brings exactly two seats, every election becomes a fight over the Court, and justices may come to be seen as partisan appointees.
args.evidence: Critics' arguments summarized in the presidential commission's report; the 2018 R Street analysis.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the Court is already a campaign issue, and predictable openings lower the stakes of each one.

args.claim: Doing it by statute may be unconstitutional.
args.warrant: The Good Behaviour Clause is widely read to guarantee life tenure. A law forcing justices off the Court could be struck down and would invite a crisis; an amendment is very hard to pass.
args.evidence: The CRS report stating that many commentators believe an amendment is required; National Constitution Center summary of the debate.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the resolution can be met by an amendment, and that some scholars argue a careful statute keeping justices in office as judges would be valid.

args.warrant: Moving to the new system means deciding what happens to sitting justices, how to fill seats that open early, and what to do if the Senate refuses to confirm. Each fix could add new disputes.
args.evidence: The presidential commission's chapter on design questions; the CRS discussion of a Court with more or fewer than nine justices during the transition.
args.response: The affirmative replies that these design questions have workable answers, such as phasing in the system with new appointees only.

strawmen.strawman: They want to pack the Court with judges who'll rule their way.
strawmen.why: Supporters across the political spectrum back 18-year terms as a neutral rule that gives every president the same number of appointments.
strawmen.steelman: Regular, staggered terms would give each president two appointments, end the role of chance and strategic retirements, and keep the Court connected to the country over time while preserving independence.

strawmen.strawman: They just like the current justices and want to keep them.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue from the Constitution's text, judicial independence and practical problems, and many proposals wouldn't affect sitting justices anyway.
strawmen.steelman: Life tenure protects judges from political and career pressure; term limits risk making every election about the Court and may require an amendment, which is very hard to pass.

weak.arg: The justices are too old to do the job.
weak.why: It's an attack on people rather than the system, and age alone says little about a judge's ability.

weak.arg: The framers chose life tenure, so it must be right forever.
weak.why: The framers also created Article V so the Constitution could be changed; argue about why life tenure still works.
